lessonTitle: Antibiotic Classes and Mechanisms of Action

blocks.text: Penicillin can cure a streptococcal throat infection in a person and yet does nothing to a human cell sitting a micrometre away. Selective toxicity means every antibiotic aims at a structure or pathway that bacteria have and humans lack, or have in a different form. Learn the targets and you can predict what an antibiotic will kill, what it will miss and why.

blocks.markdown: Antibiotics fall into a small number of target groups: **cell wall synthesis**, **protein synthesis** (bacterial 70S ribosome, with 30S and 50S subunits), **nucleic acid synthesis or integrity**, and **folate metabolism**. Humans have no peptidoglycan, a different ribosome (80S) and different gyrase and folate enzymes, which is the basis of selective toxicity.

blocks.title: Bactericidal and bacteriostatic
blocks.text: A bactericidal antibiotic kills bacteria; a bacteriostatic antibiotic inhibits growth and relies on the host immune system to clear the organism. The **minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)** is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth; the **minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC)** is the lowest that kills 99.9% of the inoculum. An MBC/MIC ratio of 4 or less is conventionally taken as bactericidal.

blocks.caption: Conventional laboratory criterion; the classification can depend on organism and conditions
Major classes, targets and activity
rows: Penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) in cell wall synthesis
Bactericidal; need oxygen-dependent uptake, so poor against anaerobes
Individually bacteriostatic; the combination is often bactericidal
Reduced to radicals that damage DNA in anaerobes

blocks.markdown: **Beta-lactams.** The beta-lactam ring mimics the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the peptide cross-link and covalently binds **penicillin-binding proteins** (PBPs), the transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan. Without cross-links the wall is weak and the cell lyses. Because killing needs active wall synthesis, activity is greatest against growing cells. **Vancomycin** instead binds the D-Ala-D-Ala substrate itself, blocking the same process by a different mechanism and is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.

blocks.title: Reading an MIC dilution series
blocks.prompt: Broth tubes contain a doubling dilution series of an antibiotic from 64 mg/L down. Tubes 1 to 4 (64, 32, 16, 8 mg/L) are clear; tube 5 (4 mg/L) is turbid. What is the MIC? When 0.1 mL from each clear tube is subcultured, only tubes 1 and 2 show no colonies. What is the MBC and the ratio?

steps.text: Concentrations: each tube is half the previous one. The lowest concentration with no visible growth is tube 4, 8 mg/L, so MIC = 8 mg/L.
Subculture shows no survivors only in tubes 1 and 2; the lowest such concentration is 32 mg/L, so MBC = 32 mg/L.

blocks.answer: MIC 8 mg/L, MBC 32 mg/L, ratio 4: conventionally bactericidal.

blocks.markdown: **Protein synthesis inhibitors.** Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit, cause misreading of mRNA and are bactericidal, but need the proton-motive force to enter and so are inactive against anaerobes. Tetracyclines bind 30S and block aminoacyl-tRNA. Macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol bind the 50S subunit. **Nucleic acid agents.** Quinolones trap DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV on DNA, breaking the chromosome; rifampicin blocks RNA polymerase. **Folate pathway.** Humans take folate from the diet, whereas bacteria must synthesise it, so sulfonamides and trimethoprim, which block sequential steps, are selectively toxic.

blocks.title: Matching class to target and effect
blocks.prompt: A drug binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and is usually bacteriostatic. What class is it and why does immune competence matter when it is used?

steps.text: 50S-binding drugs include macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol; usually bacteriostatic suggests a macrolide.
Bacteriostatic drugs stop replication but do not reliably kill, so clearance relies on host defences such as phagocytes.

blocks.answer: A macrolide (for example azithromycin); clearance depends on host immunity.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing empirically.** Before a culture result, choose a class that (i) reaches the **site**, (ii) covers the **likely organisms** for that site, and (iii) suits the patient (allergy, severity). Examples of the logic, taught here as reasoning rather than as treatment instructions: community-acquired uncomplicated cystitis is mainly Gram-negative bacilli such as *E. coli*, so agents concentrated in urine are logical; community-acquired pneumonia is commonly *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, so a beta-lactam is logical, with a macrolide or tetracycline added to cover atypical organisms (which lack a conventional wall target or live intracellularly); bacterial meningitis requires a drug that crosses the inflamed meninges and covers pneumococcus and meningococcus, such as a third-generation cephalosporin; cellulitis is mainly *Streptococcus pyogenes* and *Staphylococcus aureus*, so a beta-lactam active against both is logical.

items: DNA and RNA: quinolones (gyrase, topoisomerase IV) and rifampicin (RNA polymerase).

blocks.title: Empirical choice has three questions
blocks.text: Which organisms are likely at this site? Does the drug reach the site at an effective concentration? Is the patient able to take it safely? Then review once culture results return.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: Cidal and static are not absolute: they depend on organism, concentration and inoculum. Aminoglycosides do not work against anaerobes, and vancomycin does not work against Gram-negative bacilli. Do not choose a drug without considering the site of infection.

points: Antibiotics are selectively toxic: wall synthesis, 30S/50S ribosome, nucleic acid enzymes or folate synthesis.
Beta-lactams inhibit PBP transpeptidases; vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala.
Bactericidal agents kill; bacteriostatic agents inhibit growth and need host defences; MBC/MIC of 4 or less is bactericidal.
Empirical choice matches site, likely organisms and patient factors.

questions.stem: Which is the molecular target of beta-lactam antibiotics?

distractorRationale.b: The 30S subunit is the target of aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
distractorRationale.c: DNA gyrase is the target of quinolones.
distractorRationale.d: Dihydrofolate reductase is the target of trimethoprim.

questions.explanation: Beta-lactams covalently bind penicillin-binding proteins and prevent cross-linking of peptidoglycan. The weakened wall cannot resist osmotic pressure and the cell lyses.

questions.stem: A patient is infected with an anaerobic bacterium in an abscess. Which statement explains why gentamicin is a poor choice?

options.text: Aminoglycoside uptake needs oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes take it up poorly
Aminoglycosides target peptidoglycan, which anaerobes lack
Aminoglycosides are bacteriostatic and so cannot act in abscesses

questions.correctOptionText: Aminoglycoside uptake needs oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes take it up poorly
questions.explanation: Entry of aminoglycosides across the cytoplasmic membrane depends on the proton-motive force generated by aerobic respiration. Anaerobes lack this, so the drug does not reach its ribosomal target.

questions.stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism is correct?

options.text: Ciprofloxacin: inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

questions.correctOptionText: Ciprofloxacin: inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

distractorRationale.c: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala of cell wall precursors.

questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones trap topoisomerases on DNA and cause lethal breaks. The other pairings mix up the targets of RNA polymerase, cell wall and ribosome inhibitors.

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally bacteriostatic?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis and are generally bacteriostatic.

questions.explanation: Tetracyclines block aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the 30S subunit, halting growth without usually killing the cell. The other drugs kill bacteria by wall disruption, ribosome misreading or DNA damage.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a two-day history of dysuria and frequency with no fever or flank pain; urine dipstick is positive for nitrites. Which empirical approach follows the logic taught here?

options.text: Choose an agent active against Escherichia coli and concentrated in urine, then review against local resistance data and culture
Choose vancomycin, because it is bactericidal
Choose an aminoglycoside because anaerobes are the most likely cause
Choose a macrolide because Gram-negative bacilli lack a cell wall

questions.correctOptionText: Choose an agent active against Escherichia coli and concentrated in urine, then review against local resistance data and culture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: site and likely organism drive the choice.
distractorRationale.b: Vancomycin does not cover Gram-negative bacilli.
distractorRationale.c: Urinary infection is mostly caused by Gram-negative aerobes, not anaerobes.
distractorRationale.d: Gram-negative bacilli have a cell wall; the statement is false.

questions.explanation: Nitrite-positive cystitis is most often caused by Enterobacterales such as E. coli, so the drug should cover them and reach the urine. Local resistance patterns and culture guide any review.

questions.stem: A broth doubling dilution series starts at 256 mg/L in tube 1 (each later tube has half the concentration of the previous). Tubes 1 to 6 show no visible growth; tube 7 is turbid. Calculate the MIC in mg/L.
questions.explanation: The concentration in tube n is 256 / 2^(n-1). Tube 6 contains 256/32 = 8 mg/L and is the lowest tube without growth, so the MIC is 8 mg/L.

questions.stem: For an isolate, the MIC of an antibiotic is 2 mg/L and the MBC is 32 mg/L. Calculate the MBC/MIC ratio and give it as a number.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 32 / 2 = 16. A ratio above 4 means the drug inhibits growth at concentrations far below those that kill, so for this isolate it behaves as bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics, using MIC and MBC, and state why this may matter in a patient with severely impaired immune defences.
markingGuide: Bactericidal kills bacteria; bacteriostatic inhibits growth
MIC defined as lowest concentration preventing visible growth
MBC defined as lowest concentration killing 99.9% of the inoculum
MBC/MIC of 4 or less indicates bactericidal activity
Bacteriostatic drugs depend on host defences to clear infection, so impaired immunity makes them less reliable
questions.explanation: The distinction is practical as well as laboratory-based: static agents rely on the immune system. The MBC/MIC ratio is the quantitative marker.

questions.stem: Match each of the following to its cellular target and state whether it is generally bactericidal or bacteriostatic: a penicillin, an aminoglycoside, a macrolide, a fluoroquinolone and trimethoprim.
markingGuide: Fluoroquinolone: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal
Trimethoprim: dihydrofolate reductase (folate synthesis); generally bacteriostatic alone
questions.explanation: Each class has a defined target which explains its spectrum and toxicity. Recording cidal or static activity follows from whether the target is essential for survival or growth.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has a productive cough and fever and is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia without features of severe disease. Using the principles of empirical selection, explain how you would choose an antibiotic class, naming the likely organisms and why an additional agent may be considered for atypical organisms. Do not give doses.
markingGuide: Likely organism Streptococcus pneumoniae (also Haemophilus influenzae)
Atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) lack a conventional cell wall target or are intracellular, so a macrolide or tetracycline may be added
Consider patient factors such as allergy and severity and review when microbiology returns
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy matches the site and probable organisms. Atypical organisms are not reliably covered by beta-lactams, which explains the addition of a drug acting on protein synthesis.
